en.title: Agronomy: the whole course
en.short: What agronomy is, how the degree is organised, the main areas in teaching order, and how to study it.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text:
Agronomy is the science and practice of growing crops in the field. It brings together plant science, soil science, weather, pests and weeds, and the economics of the farm to answer one practical question: how should a crop be grown, in a particular place, to give a good and reliable yield without destroying the soil?

It sits beside horticulture, which deals mainly with fruits, vegetables and ornamentals, and beside animal science. Agronomy is broader than crop science alone because it studies the whole field system: soil, water, crop, pests, labour and machinery together.

The subject is both biological and managerial. A result from plant physiology only becomes agronomy when it is tested in a field, under a farmer’s conditions, and shown to pay.

sections.heading: How a degree is usually organised
sections.text:
Length and awards differ by country and institution, so always check your own handbook. In Nigeria, universities commonly offer a four- or five-year BSc or BAgric in agronomy, crop science or agriculture, under benchmarks set by the National Universities Commission. Polytechnics, regulated by the National Board for Technical Education, award the ND and HND; colleges of education award the NCE. In Ghana and Kenya a bachelor’s degree is commonly four years; in the United Kingdom three years, often four in Scotland.

The pattern is similar everywhere: foundation science in the first year, production subjects in the middle years, and a project or dissertation at the end. A master’s degree adds theory, research methods and a dissertation.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
The course follows the way a crop is grown. It starts with foundations: what agronomy is and its history; plant structure and function; photosynthesis, respiration and growth; seed germination and establishment; soil formation, physical properties and classification; soil chemistry, cation exchange and fertility; plant nutrition and nutrient cycling; weather, climate and the crop microclimate; field measurement, units and calculations; and crop classification and adaptation.

The core follows the field season: land preparation and tillage; sowing and stand establishment; water requirements and irrigation; fertilisers and integrated nutrient management; weeds; pests; diseases; environmental stress; cropping systems such as rotation and intercropping; agroforestry, cover crops and conservation agriculture; pasture and forage; soil conservation and erosion control; harvesting and postharvest handling; quality and grading; crop improvement and seed systems; farm planning, budgets and machinery; precision agriculture and mechanisation; extension and adoption; research methods and field trials; and professional ethics, safety and regulation.

At master’s level the course turns to advanced crop physiology and modelling, soil-plant nutrient dynamics, climate change and sustainable systems, and the research frontier that leads to your dissertation.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Study agronomy by connecting the laboratory to the field. For each topic, ask what a farmer would do differently because of it. Learn the vocabulary precisely: cation exchange capacity, leaf area index, harvest index, field capacity. Each has a precise definition; some are ratios without units.

Practise the calculations until they are automatic: plant population from spacing, seed rate, fertiliser rates from nutrient percentage, water depth from volume and area. Check every answer against a rough estimate.

Read a textbook chapter, then look at a real field or a trial plot. Keep a notebook of observations: dates, weather, crop stage, pest counts. Learn the scientific names of the main crops, weeds and pests you meet. Use past examination questions and, for research methods, read one field trial report and identify its design, treatments and error control.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Students memorise definitions without being able to apply them. They confuse soil texture with structure, and soil fertility with fertiliser. They mix up units, especially kg/ha, kg per plant and grams per plot, and forget to convert plot yields to hectares.

Many describe a pest or disease but cannot name the damage it causes or the threshold for spraying. Others recommend a practice without saying for which soil, climate or crop.

In field trials, students confuse replication with repeated measurements, and forget randomisation. In reports, they state conclusions beyond what the data show. Finally, do not quote a yield, a price or a fertiliser recommendation without its country, year and source. These change.

keyPoints: Agronomy studies how to grow crops in the field, combining plant, soil, weather and management knowledge.
Degree length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook.
The course moves from plant and soil foundations to field production, then to research and advanced study.
Learn each term with its definition and, where it has one, its unit.
Practise agronomic calculations and check every answer against a rough estimate.
Never quote a yield, price or recommendation without its country, year and source.

en.title: Agronomy as a Discipline: Scope, History and Systems View
en.short: Agronomy defined, its neighbours, the field as a system, and the shift from tradition to research.

sections.heading: What agronomy is
sections.text:
Agronomy is the science and practice of growing field crops. It studies how soil, crop, weather and management work together to produce grain, roots, fibre and fodder at field scale. The word comes from Greek agros (field) and nomos (management).

Soil science studies the soil itself; crop science studies the crop plant, its physiology and genetics; horticulture covers fruit, vegetables and ornamentals, usually on small, intensive plots; agricultural extension is the education work that helps farmers adopt new practice. Agronomy is the integrative one: it asks how the whole field is managed.

sections.heading: The field as a system
sections.text:
The field is a system: the four factors interact, so a change in one alters the others. Soil supplies water, air, nutrients and anchorage. The plant responds with growth, and crops and varieties differ. Weather sets the limits of temperature, rainfall and light. Management is the human lever: crop and variety choice, sowing date, spacing, fertiliser, weeding, harvest.

Case: Amina grows maize on sandy loam near Kaduna, Nigeria. One season the rains start late. Sowing on the usual date would put seed into dry soil, so she waits for the first reliable rain and sows a shorter-season variety. Weather and soil have shifted; only a management decision can match them.

sections.heading: From practice to science
sections.text:
Farming knowledge is older than agricultural science. Farmers learned by trial and error: rotating crops, resting land in fallow, mixing crops, terracing slopes, saving seed from the best plants. Such practice is often well matched to local conditions.

Modern agronomy began when this experience met systematic experiment. In the 1840s Justus von Liebig argued that plants feed on mineral nutrients, and Rothamsted Experimental Station in England began long-term trials that still run today. Replicated field trials, plant breeding and fertiliser chemistry followed. The Green Revolution of the mid twentieth century raised wheat and rice yields sharply in Asia, with uneven benefits and costs. Today agronomy tests recommendations in farmers’ fields and re-examines traditional practice.

keyPoints: Agronomy is the integrative science of managing field crop systems; soil science, crop science, horticulture and extension each study one part of that system.
A field is a system of four interacting factors: soil, plant, weather and management, and management is the one the farmer controls directly.
Traditional farming knowledge came from long trial and error and remains a source of locally tested practice.
Modern agronomy rests on replicated field experiments, mineral nutrition theory and plant breeding, dating from the nineteenth century.
The Green Revolution raised cereal yields sharply in parts of Asia, but its benefits and costs were uneven.
A recommendation must be tested in local soil and climate, because a practice that works in one place may fail in another.

en.title: Plant Structure and Function for Crop Production
en.short: Shoot, root, leaf and vascular anatomy, and how pruning, thinning, transplanting and defoliation affect crops.

sections.heading: Shoot and root systems
sections.text: A crop has a shoot system above ground and a root system below. The shoot is the stem, leaves and buds. It grows from apical meristems, dividing tissues at the tips, and from axillary buds at nodes, the points where leaves attach. The stem’s internodes separate nodes and hold leaves in light. Apical dominance is the suppression of side buds by the terminal bud. Roots anchor the plant, absorb water and minerals, and store food. Root hairs are fine extensions that greatly increase absorbing surface. A taproot is one main root; a fibrous root system is many similar roots.

sections.heading: Leaf and vascular tissues
sections.text: The leaf has a blade, often a petiole, and veins. Its epidermis has a waxy cuticle that limits water loss, and stomata, small pores that open for gas exchange. Mesophyll is the photosynthetic tissue inside. The vascular system is continuous through roots, stems and leaves. Xylem carries water and dissolved minerals upward; phloem carries sugars from leaves to growing and storage parts. Veins therefore supply leaves and export their sugar. Leaf area captures light, while the vascular network and stomata keep that surface supplied and cooled.

sections.heading: Field operations
sections.text: These structures explain field operations. Pruning removes branches or buds, reducing apical dominance and letting light reach side shoots. Thinning removes crowded plants so the survivors have more water, nutrients and light. Transplanting moves seedlings; root hairs are often damaged, so water uptake falls and leaves may wilt until new roots grow. Defoliation removes leaves, cutting photosynthesis and yield, though some crops are defoliated deliberately before harvest. In a tomato nursery, seedlings lifted with bare roots lose root hairs; water them at once and shade them briefly to reduce water loss.

keyPoints: Apical meristems at shoot and root tips produce new cells for growth.
Nodes bear leaves and axillary buds; internodes separate nodes.
Xylem moves water and minerals upward; phloem moves sugars.
Root hairs increase absorption, and transplanting often damages them.
Pruning and thinning change competition and light; defoliation reduces photosynthesis.
Stomata and the cuticle regulate gas exchange and water loss.

en.title: Photosynthesis, Respiration, Growth and Development
en.short: Carbon gain and loss, dry matter, growth analysis, hormones and photoperiodic flowering.

sections.heading: Carbon balance
sections.text: Photosynthesis uses light energy to convert carbon dioxide and water into sugars, releasing oxygen. Respiration oxidises sugars to release energy for maintenance and growth, giving off carbon dioxide and water. Dry matter is what remains after water is removed. Net dry matter accumulation depends on the carbon balance: gross photosynthesis minus respiration. A crop gains dry matter only when carbon fixed exceeds carbon lost.

sections.heading: Growth and development
sections.text: Growth is an increase in size, mass or cell number. Development is progress through growth stages: germination, leaf production, tillering or branching, flowering, grain filling and maturity. A crop may grow without developing normally, or develop while growth slows. Yield depends on both the amount of dry matter made and how it is distributed among roots, stems, leaves and grain.

sections.heading: Growth analysis
sections.text: Growth analysis uses simple measures. Leaf area index (LAI) is leaf area divided by ground area; LAI 4 means 4 m² leaf per 1 m² ground. Crop growth rate (CGR) is dry matter increase per ground area per day, often g m−2 day−1. Harvest index (HI) is economic yield divided by total above-ground dry matter. Example: dry matter rises from 200 to 350 g m−2 in 10 days, so CGR = (350 − 200) ÷ 10 = 15 g m−2 day−1. If grain is 180 g m−2 and total above-ground dry matter is 450 g m−2, HI = 180 ÷ 450 = 0.40, or 40%.

sections.heading: Hormones and flowering
sections.text: Plant hormones are chemical signals. Auxins promote cell elongation and root formation; gibberellins promote stem elongation and seed germination; cytokinins promote cell division; abscisic acid slows growth and closes stomata in drought; ethylene ripens fruit and promotes leaf fall. Photoperiod is the daily length of light and dark. It controls flowering in many crops: short-day plants flower when days are short and nights long, long-day plants when days are long and nights short, and day-neutral plants are less sensitive.

keyPoints: Net dry matter = gross photosynthesis − respiration.
Growth is increase in size or mass; development is progress through growth stages.
LAI = leaf area ÷ ground area.
CGR = (W2 − W1) ÷ (t2 − t1), in g m−2 day−1.
Harvest index = economic yield ÷ total above-ground dry matter.
Photoperiod and hormones control flowering; short-day plants flower when nights are long.

en.title: Seed Science, Germination and Crop Establishment
en.short: Seed structure, quality, germination, dormancy, testing, storage and field establishment.

sections.heading: Seed structure and quality
sections.text: A seed contains an embryo, stored food and a protective coat. In dicots the food is mainly in cotyledons; in cereals it is in the endosperm. The seed coat or testa protects the embryo. Viability is the ability to germinate under favourable conditions. Vigour is the ability to germinate, emerge and grow well, including under stress. Two lots can have the same viability but different vigour.

sections.heading: Germination and dormancy
sections.text: Germination needs water for imbibition, oxygen for respiration and a suitable temperature; some seeds also need light or darkness. Dormancy is when a viable seed fails to germinate although conditions seem suitable. It may be physical, from a hard seed coat, or physiological, needing after-ripening or chilling. Dormancy spreads germination in time, but it can delay crop establishment.

sections.heading: Testing, certification and storage
sections.text: Seed testing measures purity, germination percentage, moisture and sometimes vigour. Certification is an official system that checks genetic identity and quality and allows a label to be attached. Store orthodox seeds cool, dry and protected from pests; high moisture and heat shorten life. Recalcitrant seeds, such as cocoa, cannot be dried and stored cold.

sections.heading: Field consequences
sections.text: Sowing rate should be calculated from the target plant population and expected field establishment. For 200,000 plants/ha, with 95% purity, 90% germination and 80% field survival, establishment is 0.95 × 0.90 × 0.80 = 0.684. Seeds needed = 200,000 ÷ 0.684 = 292,398 per ha. At 40 g per 1,000 seeds, that is 292,398 × 40 ÷ 1,000 = 11.7 kg/ha. Sow deep enough to reach moisture but not so deep that reserves run out before emergence. Seed treatment controls seed-borne disease and pests; legume inoculants add rhizobia. Direct seeding suits large areas and good seedbeds; transplanting saves seed and can improve early stand, but costs labour and causes transplant shock.

keyPoints: A seed has an embryo, stored food and a protective coat; viability is ability to germinate, vigour is ability to perform well, including under stress.
Germination requires water, oxygen and a suitable temperature, and some seeds also need light or darkness.
Dormancy is a viable seed failing to germinate under apparently suitable conditions; it may be physical or physiological.
Seed testing measures purity, germination, moisture and vigour; certification is an official quality and identity check.
Store orthodox seed cool, dry and pest-free; recalcitrant seed cannot be dried and stored cold.
Sowing rate = target population ÷ (purity × germination × field survival), and seed mass = seeds × 1,000-seed weight ÷ 1,000.

en.title: Soil Formation, Physical Properties and Classification
en.short: How soils form and are classified, and how texture, structure, density and water capacity guide tillage and irrigation.

sections.heading: Formation and profile
sections.text: Soil forms from parent material under climate, organisms, relief and time. These are the five soil-forming factors. Parent material supplies minerals; climate drives weathering and organic matter; organisms mix and decompose; relief, or topography, affects drainage and erosion; time allows horizons to develop. A soil profile is a vertical section with horizons: O organic, A topsoil, E leached, B subsoil accumulation, C weathered parent material, R bedrock. Not every soil has all horizons.

sections.heading: Texture and structure
sections.text: Texture is the proportion of sand, silt and clay particles under 2 mm. It is named on a texture triangle, for example sandy loam or clay loam. Structure is how particles bind into aggregates; describe grade (how distinct the aggregates are), size and shape. Good structure aids roots, air and water.

sections.heading: Density, porosity and water
sections.text:
Bulk density is oven-dry soil mass divided by total volume, in g/cm³. Porosity is the fraction of volume that is pores: porosity = 1 − bulk density ÷ particle density. Mineral particle density is often about 2.65 g/cm³. Water holding capacity: field capacity is water held after drainage; wilting point is water too tightly held for plants; available water capacity is the difference.

Worked example: a 100 cm³ core weighs 130 g dry. Bulk density = 130 ÷ 100 = 1.30 g/cm³. Porosity = 1 − 1.30 ÷ 2.65 = 0.51, or 51%. If field capacity is 0.30 and wilting point 0.12 m³/m³, available water = 0.18 m³/m³; over a 60 cm root zone, 0.18 × 600 mm = 108 mm.

sections.heading: Classification and management
sections.text: Classification groups soils by properties and genesis. Widely used systems include USDA Soil Taxonomy and the World Reference Base; many countries also have their own national systems, so names differ. Texture and structure set choices. Sandy soils drain fast, hold little water and need frequent small irrigation; clay soils hold more water but tillage when wet can compact them. Tillage should suit structure and moisture; irrigation scheduling should use available water capacity, not guesswork. Check local soil survey and current recommendations.

keyPoints: Soil forms from parent material under climate, organisms, relief and time, producing horizons in a profile.
Texture is the sand, silt and clay proportions; structure is how particles form aggregates.
Bulk density = oven-dry mass ÷ total volume; porosity = 1 − bulk density ÷ particle density.
Available water capacity = field capacity − wilting point, and it sets irrigation amounts.
Texture and structure guide tillage: avoid tilling wet clay, and irrigate sandy soils in smaller, more frequent doses.
Soil classification systems differ by country and organisation, so check the local system and soil survey.

en.title: Soil Chemistry, Cation Exchange and Soil Fertility
en.short: Soil colloids, CEC, base saturation, pH and buffering, fertility versus productivity, and soil testing.

sections.heading: Colloids and CEC
sections.text: Clay particles and humus are soil colloids: very small particles with a large surface area. Negative charges on their surfaces hold cations such as Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, K⁺ and Na⁺. Other cations in the soil solution can replace them, and this is cation exchange. The total exchangeable charge a soil can hold is its cation exchange capacity (CEC), measured in cmol(+)/kg (the older unit is meq/100 g).

sections.heading: pH, bases and buffering
sections.text: Base saturation is the percentage of the CEC occupied by basic cations (Ca, Mg, K, Na). Soil pH measures acidity in the soil solution. Soils resist pH change because colloids release or take up ions; this is buffering. Nutrient availability depends on pH: most nutrients are available near pH 6 to 7, phosphorus is fixed in strongly acid and strongly alkaline soils, and at low pH aluminium can be toxic.

sections.heading: Fertility and testing
sections.text: Soil fertility is the ability to supply available nutrients. Soil productivity is the capacity to produce crop yields, which also depends on water, climate, pests and management, so a fertile soil can be unproductive. Laboratory tests measure pH (in water and in KCl), CEC and exchangeable bases, organic carbon, available phosphorus and texture. Field methods include sampling by grid or by soil type, and field trials that calibrate test values against yield. Grades and thresholds differ by country and crop, so check the current national soil-test guide.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
A soil has CEC 20 cmol(+)/kg. Exchangeable Ca = 8, Mg = 3, K = 0.5 and Na = 0.5 cmol(+)/kg.
Sum of bases = 8 + 3 + 0.5 + 0.5 = 12 cmol(+)/kg.
Base saturation = 12 ÷ 20 × 100 = 60%.

keyPoints: Soil colloids (clay and humus) carry negative charges that hold cations.
CEC is the total exchangeable cations a soil can hold, in cmol(+)/kg.
Base saturation = (sum of exchangeable basic cations ÷ CEC) × 100.
pH controls nutrient availability; near pH 6 to 7 most nutrients are available.
Fertility is the ability to supply nutrients; productivity is the capacity to produce yields.
Soil test values must be calibrated locally by field trials before use.

en.title: Plant Nutrition and Nutrient Cycling
en.short: Essential nutrients, uptake, deficiency and toxicity signs, and the carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus cycles.

sections.heading: Essential nutrients
sections.text:
Plants need 17 or so essential elements. Macronutrients are carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium and sulphur. Micronutrients include iron, manganese, zinc, copper, boron, molybdenum, chlorine and nickel. Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen come mainly from air and water; the others from soil.

Nitrogen builds proteins and chlorophyll; deficiency pales older leaves. Phosphorus supports energy transfer and roots; deficiency stunts and darkens or purples older leaves. Potassium regulates water and enzymes; deficiency scorches leaf margins. Calcium builds cell walls; deficiency distorts new leaves. Magnesium sits inside the chlorophyll molecule and iron helps build chlorophyll; deficiency yellows between veins, young leaves for iron and older for magnesium. Excess boron burns margins; excess nitrogen makes soft, lodging growth.

sections.heading: Uptake and cycles
sections.text:
Roots absorb nutrient ions from the soil solution by root interception, mass flow and diffusion. Most ions enter by active transport, which uses energy. Mycorrhizal fungi extend roots and aid phosphorus and zinc uptake.

The nitrogen cycle moves N between organic matter, ammonium, nitrate, plants and air. Mineralisation releases ammonium; nitrification forms nitrate; leaching and denitrification lose N. The phosphorus cycle has no gas phase; weathering, adsorption and erosion control supply, so P is often limiting. The carbon cycle begins with photosynthesis fixing carbon dioxide; respiration and decomposition release it.

sections.heading: Fixation and organic matter
sections.text:
Biological nitrogen fixation converts atmospheric nitrogen gas into ammonia using nitrogenase, an enzyme needing iron and molybdenum. Rhizobium bacteria in legume root nodules are the main farm example; some free-living bacteria and Frankia also fix nitrogen. Fixed N enters the crop and later the soil.

Organic matter feeds crops through decomposition. Microbes break residues into simpler compounds, release nutrients and build humus. The carbon-to-nitrogen ratio matters: residues above about 25:1 can immobilise nitrogen at first, as microbes tie up soil N while decomposing them; low ratios mineralise it.

sections.heading: Field case
sections.text: Case: Ada in Enugu grows maize after cowpea. Cowpea fixes nitrogen and its residues decompose. If she leaves maize stover with a high C:N ratio, early maize may yellow from temporary N immobilisation. Young, leafy residues help.

keyPoints: Macronutrients are needed in larger amounts than micronutrients, but both are essential.
Deficiency symptoms often show first on old or young leaves depending on whether the nutrient is mobile.
Roots take up ions by interception, mass flow and diffusion, mostly through active transport.
Biological nitrogen fixation by Rhizobium in legumes converts N2 gas to ammonia.
High C:N residues can immobilise nitrogen; low C:N residues release it.
Excess nutrients can be toxic, for example boron burning leaf margins.

en.title: Weather, Climate and the Crop Microclimate
en.short: Weather elements, evapotranspiration, growing degree days and how shelter, mulch and spacing alter crop microclimate.

sections.heading: Weather elements
sections.text: Crop growth is driven by weather: the state of the atmosphere at a place and time. Solar radiation supplies energy for photosynthesis and warms leaves and soil. Temperature controls enzyme activity, germination and development rate. Rainfall supplies water, but timing and intensity matter as much as total. Humidity is water vapour in the air; high humidity slows evaporation and can favour some diseases. Wind moves heat, vapour and carbon dioxide, and strong wind damages plants and dries soil.

sections.heading: Evapotranspiration and heat
sections.text:
Evapotranspiration (ET) is water lost as vapour from soil and plant surfaces (evaporation) plus water lost through leaf pores (transpiration). It depends on radiation, temperature, humidity, wind and soil water. When soil water is limited, ET falls and growth slows.

Growing degree days (GDD) measure accumulated heat. Use GDD = Σ[(Tmax + Tmin) ÷ 2 − Tbase], counting only days above Tbase. Example: Tmax = 32 °C, Tmin = 18 °C, Tbase = 10 °C. Mean = (32 + 18) ÷ 2 = 25 °C. Daily GDD = 25 − 10 = 15. Over five days, GDD = 5 × 15 = 75 degree days.

sections.heading: Climate and microclimate
sections.text: Climate is the average weather pattern of a region over many years, including usual range and extremes. It sets which crops can be grown. Microclimate is the conditions close to the crop, within or above the canopy. It differs from regional climate because of plant cover, soil colour, slope, shelter and irrigation. A maize canopy, for example, is cooler, more humid and less windy than open field.

sections.heading: Modifying the microclimate
sections.text: Windbreaks are rows of trees or tall crops that slow wind. They cut mechanical damage and evaporation, but may shade crops and compete for water. Mulch is material spread on the soil surface. It lowers soil temperature, conserves water and suppresses weeds. Spacing changes canopy density: closer rows shade soil and weeds, while wider rows increase airflow and reduce humidity. Choose these tools for local climate and crop.

keyPoints: Weather is the short-term state of the atmosphere; climate is the long-term average pattern of a region.
Solar radiation, temperature, rainfall, humidity and wind are the main weather elements affecting crops.
Evapotranspiration is evaporation from soil and plant surfaces plus transpiration through leaves.
Growing degree days accumulate heat: GDD = Σ[(Tmax + Tmin) ÷ 2 − Tbase], counting days above Tbase.
Microclimate is the conditions within or near the crop canopy, and it can differ strongly from regional climate.
Windbreaks, mulch and row spacing modify wind, temperature, humidity and soil water in the crop microclimate.

en.title: Field Measurement, Units and Agronomic Calculations
en.short: Hectares, seed and fertiliser rates, plot yields, sampling and unit conversions, with checked worked calculations.

sections.heading: Units and area
sections.text:
Agronomists measure land in hectares (ha). One hectare is 10,000 square metres (m²), a square 100 m by 100 m. One acre is about 0.4047 ha, so 1 ha is about 2.47 acres. Yield is mass per area, usually kilograms per hectare (kg/ha) or tonnes per ha; 1 tonne = 1,000 kg, so 1 t/ha = 1,000 kg/ha. Also 1 kg/ha = 0.1 g/m², because 1,000 g is spread over 10,000 m².

Worked example: a field 120 m long and 75 m wide.
Area = 120 × 75 = 9,000 m²
In hectares: 9,000 ÷ 10,000 = 0.9 ha

sections.heading: Seed and fertiliser rates
sections.text:
Rates are quoted per hectare, then scaled to the plot. Fertiliser advice is usually given in kg of nutrient, not kg of product, so divide by the nutrient fraction.

Example: 60 kg N/ha from urea, which is 46% N.
Urea = 60 ÷ 0.46 = 130.4 kg/ha
Check: 130.4 × 0.46 = 60.0 kg N
For the 0.9 ha field: 130.4 × 0.9 = 117.4 kg urea

Seed rate follows from the target plant population. At 75 cm × 25 cm spacing:
Plants/ha = 10,000 ÷ (0.75 × 0.25) = 10,000 ÷ 0.1875 = 53,333
With 90% field germination: 53,333 ÷ 0.90 = 59,259 seeds/ha
If 1,000 seeds weigh 300 g: 59,259 × 0.3 g = 17.8 kg/ha

sections.heading: Plots, sampling and yield
sections.text:
Mark plots with tape and pegs, and keep the measured shape simple. Discard border rows (guard rows), because edge plants grow differently from the rest. For yield, harvest a known area, weigh it, and convert to the hectare.

Example: a plot 5 m × 4 m = 20 m² gives 3.2 kg of grain.
Yield = 3.2 ÷ 20 = 0.16 kg/m²
Per hectare: 0.16 × 10,000 = 1,600 kg/ha = 1.6 t/ha

For sampling, use several small quadrats (measured frames) placed at random, not just the best corner. Repeat readings, check tape and balance, and write the unit beside every number.

sections.heading: Records and error
sections.text: Record the date, field, plot area, product, rate and unit on the same day, in a notebook or spreadsheet. Common errors are mixed units, miscounted plots and grain moisture. State the moisture content whenever you report yield, since wet grain weighs more.

keyPoints: 1 ha = 10,000 m²; 1 t/ha = 1,000 kg/ha; 1 kg/ha = 0.1 g/m².
Product rate = nutrient rate ÷ nutrient fraction, for example urea at 46% N.
Plants per ha = 10,000 ÷ (row spacing × within-row spacing in metres).
Yield (kg/ha) = harvest weight (kg) ÷ plot area (m²) × 10,000.
Use several random quadrats, discard guard rows, and state grain moisture.
Write date, plot area, product, rate and unit in the record the same day.

en.title: Crop Classification, Adaptation and Growth Habit
en.short: Grouping crops by use, life cycle and family, and matching adaptation, growth habit and cropping systems.

sections.heading: Classifying by use
sections.text:
Field crops are grouped by use. Cereals are grasses grown for grain, such as maize. Grain legumes are grown for seed and often fix nitrogen with rhizobia, soil bacteria in their root nodules. Oil crops are grown for oil, such as groundnut and oil palm. Fibre crops give lint or fibre, such as cotton. Sugar crops store sugar, such as sugarcane. Roots and tubers are grown for storage organs, such as cassava and yam. Forages and pasture feed livestock. Plantation crops are long-lived tree or estate crops, such as cocoa and rubber.

Soybean is both a grain legume and an oil crop.

sections.heading: Life cycle and family
sections.text:
Life cycle describes how long a crop takes. An annual completes its life in one season, for example maize. A biennial grows vegetatively in the first season and flowers in the second, for example sugar beet. A perennial lives for several years, for example oil palm.

Botanical family groups crops by structure and reproduction. Poaceae are grasses, including cereals. Fabaceae are legumes. Solanaceae include potato and tomato. Euphorbiaceae include cassava. Related crops share pests and diseases, so they should not be rotated together.

sections.heading: Adaptation and habit
sections.text:
Agro-ecological adaptation is the fit between a crop and its environment: rainfall, temperature, day length, soil and altitude. A crop adapted to dry savanna may fail in humid forest.

Growth habit is the plant’s form and behaviour: erect or prostrate (flat on the ground), determinate or indeterminate, rooting depth and branching. Determinate crops stop vegetative growth when flowering begins; indeterminate crops keep growing. Habit affects spacing, weeding and harvest timing.

sections.heading: Patterns and systems
sections.text:
A cropping pattern is the arrangement of crops in space and time on a field, such as sole (one crop alone), mixed or intercropping. A cropping system is the wider set of patterns and practices used on a farm over years, including rotation, tillage and inputs.

Case: Amina farms near Kano, Nigeria. She plants sorghum and cowpea in alternate rows, an intercropping pattern. She rotates with groundnut and uses cattle manure. These form part of her cropping system.

keyPoints: Crops can be grouped by use, life cycle or botanical family, and one crop may belong to several use groups.
Annuals complete their life in one season, biennials in two, and perennials live for several years.
Related crops in the same family often share pests and diseases, so rotation should avoid close relatives.
Agro-ecological adaptation is the match between a crop and climate, soil and day length.
Growth habit includes erect or prostrate form, determinate or indeterminate flowering, and rooting depth.
A cropping pattern is the field arrangement; a cropping system is the farm’s wider set of patterns and practices over years.

en.title: Land Preparation and Tillage Systems
en.short: Primary and secondary tillage, compaction and erosion, tillage systems, ridging and timing.

sections.heading: Primary and secondary tillage
sections.text:
Primary tillage opens soil to depth and buries weeds and residues; implements include the mouldboard plough, disc plough, chisel plough, subsoiler and hand hoe. Secondary tillage is shallower: harrows, cultivators, rotavators and rollers break clods and level the seedbed.

Tillage breaks aggregates. Some loosening aids roots and water entry, but ploughing at the same depth forms a compact plough pan, and wheel traffic compacts the surface. Porosity = 1 − (bulk density ÷ particle density). At particle density 2.65 g/cm³, bulk density rising from 1.2 to 1.6 g/cm³ cuts porosity from 55% to 40%. Bare soil erodes faster.

sections.heading: Comparing tillage systems
sections.text:
Conventional tillage inverts the topsoil with a plough and several harrowings. It controls weeds and gives an even seedbed, but burns fuel, oxidises organic matter and exposes soil.

Minimum tillage cuts the number of passes. Conservation tillage is the umbrella term for systems that disturb soil little and keep residue on the surface; a common convention is at least about 30% cover after planting. No-till, the extreme case, sows into undisturbed soil. They save fuel and protect structure, but often need more herbicide and careful residue management.

sections.heading: Ridging and mounding
sections.text: Ridging heaps soil into raised rows. It drains heavy soils, warms the bed and suits tuber crops. Mounding heaps soil into mounds in which crops such as yam or cassava are planted, for support and rooting. Tie-ridging adds cross-ties of soil along the furrow at intervals, making basins that trap rain; it is used in semi-arid West Africa to cut runoff.

sections.heading: Timing and soil moisture
sections.text: Till when the soil is moist but workable. Too wet, and implements and tyres smear and compact it; too dry, and clods are hard and draft is high. Field test: squeeze a handful into a ball; it should crumble when pressed, not ribbon out between the fingers. Do primary tillage when moisture is adequate and secondary tillage close to sowing. In rain-fed farming, prepare land before the rains and sow soon after the first effective rain.

keyPoints: Primary tillage loosens soil to depth; secondary tillage refines the seedbed.
Repeated ploughing at one depth forms a plough pan, and traffic compacts the surface.
Porosity = 1 − (bulk density ÷ particle density), so compaction lowers porosity.
Conventional tillage inverts soil; minimum tillage disturbs less, and conservation tillage also keeps residue cover.
Ridging, mounding and tie-ridging shape soil for drainage, rooting or trapping rain.
Till only when soil is moist but workable, and finish seedbed preparation close to sowing.

en.title: Sowing, Planting and Stand Establishment
en.short: Sowing date, seed rate, spacing, depth, population, transplanting and aftercare for crop stands.

sections.heading: Setting the stand
sections.text: Sowing date is chosen so that germination, flowering and grain filling meet favourable weather and avoid peak pests. Sowing date also affects crop cycle and harvest timing. Seed rate is the weight of seed sown per hectare. It is set from target plant population, seed weight, germination percentage and expected field establishment. Spacing is the distance between rows and between plants; population density is plants per unit area. Planting depth must place seed in moist soil but allow emergence. Too deep wastes seed; too shallow risks drying. These choices differ by crop, soil, climate and local recommendation.

sections.heading: Cereals and legumes
sections.text: For cereals, calculate seed rate from target plants. Example: target 250 plants/m², seed weight 0.04 g, germination 90%, establishment 80%. Seeds needed = 250 ÷ (0.90 × 0.80) = 347/m². Seed mass = 347 × 0.04 = 13.9 g/m². Seed rate = 13.9 × 10 = 139 kg/ha. Spacing sets population: maize spaced 75 cm × 25 cm gives 10,000 ÷ (75 × 25) = 5.3 plants/m². For legumes, use larger seed and lower population; inoculate with compatible rhizobia where the soil lacks the right bacteria, and use registered seed dressings. Do not mix inoculant with incompatible dressing. Check labels.

sections.heading: Vegetatively propagated crops and aftercare
sections.text: Cassava is planted from stem cuttings; yam from setts or small tubers. Use clean, healthy material, plant at a depth and angle that keeps nodes viable, and space to the target stand. Transplanting moves seedlings from nursery to field; harden them and keep roots moist. Gap filling replaces failures early with the same variety. Thinning removes excess plants so survivors reach the target density. Record dates, rates and depths. Local extension recommendations and product labels are the final guide.

keyPoints: Sowing date matches crop development to weather, pests and harvest timing.
Seed rate (kg/ha) = 10 × target plants/m² × seed weight per seed (g) ÷ (germination fraction × establishment fraction).
Population density (plants/m²) = 10,000 ÷ (row spacing cm × within-row spacing cm).
Planting depth must balance moist soil with successful emergence; local recommendations vary.
Legumes may need compatible rhizobia inoculant; follow label compatibility with seed dressings.
Transplant, gap fill and thin early so the target stand is reached before competition.

en.title: Crop Water Requirements and Irrigation
en.short: Soil water limits, crop and irrigation requirement, irrigation methods, scheduling, efficiency and drainage.

sections.heading: Soil water storage
sections.text: The soil-plant-atmosphere continuum is the path water takes from soil to root, stem, leaf and atmosphere, driven by water potential gradients. Field capacity is the water left after excess gravitational water drains. Permanent wilting point is the water content at which a plant stays wilted. Available water is field capacity minus permanent wilting point. These limits are conventions, often near −33 kPa and −1500 kPa, and vary with soil texture.

sections.heading: Crop and irrigation requirement
sections.text: Crop water requirement is water lost by transpiration plus soil evaporation, called crop evapotranspiration (ETc). A common estimate is ETc = Kc × ETo, where ETo is reference evapotranspiration and Kc is a crop coefficient. Irrigation requirement is what must be supplied after effective rainfall and stored soil water are counted. If ETo is 5 mm/day, Kc is 1.0 and effective rainfall is 2 mm/day, ETc = 5 × 1.0 = 5 mm/day. Net irrigation = 5 − 2 = 3 mm/day. At 75% application efficiency, gross irrigation = 3 ÷ 0.75 = 4 mm/day, or 40 m³/ha/day.

sections.heading: Irrigation methods
sections.text: Surface irrigation flows water over the field by gravity. It is cheap but uneven on unlevelled land and can waste water, erode soil and waterlog low spots. Sprinkler irrigation sprays water under pressure. It suits irregular fields but loses water to wind and evaporation and needs energy. Drip irrigation delivers small, frequent amounts through emitters to the root zone. It usually gives the highest water use efficiency, but emitters clog and capital cost is high.

sections.heading: Scheduling and drainage
sections.text: Irrigation scheduling decides when and how much to apply. Use soil moisture checks or replace ETc before stress reduces yield, and avoid overwatering. Water use efficiency is yield or biomass per unit of water used; application efficiency is the share of applied water stored for the crop. Waterlogged fields lack oxygen in the root zone. Open drains, subsurface drains and raised beds remove excess water; keep outlets clear.

keyPoints: The soil-plant-atmosphere continuum moves water from soil to roots to leaves to atmosphere along water potential gradients.
Available water = field capacity − permanent wilting point.
Crop water requirement is ETc = Kc × ETo; irrigation requirement subtracts effective rainfall and stored soil water.
Net irrigation is the crop requirement not met by rain or storage; gross irrigation = net ÷ application efficiency.
Drip usually uses water most efficiently, sprinkler is flexible, and surface is cheap but uneven.
Schedule by soil moisture or ET replacement, and drain waterlogged fields to restore root oxygen.

en.title: Fertilisers and Integrated Nutrient Management
en.short: Manure and fertiliser types, label reading, application rates, placement, timing and ISFM.

sections.heading: Manures and fertilisers
sections.text: Organic manures are bulky (farmyard manure, compost, crop residues, green manure) or concentrated (poultry litter, oilseed cake, blood meal). Nutrient content is low and variable, so test or use book values cautiously. They release nutrients slowly and add organic matter, improving structure, water holding and biological activity. Inorganic fertilisers are straight (one nutrient, such as urea, 46% N), compound (chemically combined) or blended (physically mixed). A grade 20-10-10 means 20% N, 10% P2O5 and 10% K2O by mass; some countries label elemental P and K, so check the local convention. Solubility, salt injury risk and tendency to acidify soil vary.

sections.heading: Labels and application rates
sections.text: Read the net mass, grade, nutrient forms and warnings. Product rate = nutrient recommendation ÷ nutrient fraction. Example: with 20-10-10 and a recommendation of 60 kg N/ha, product = 60 ÷ 0.20 = 300 kg/ha, or six 50 kg bags. This supplies 300 × 0.10 = 30 kg P2O5/ha and 30 kg K2O/ha. Check: 300 × 0.20 = 60 kg N. From urea (46% N), 60 kg N/ha needs 60 ÷ 0.46 = 130 kg/ha, rounded. Convert to the same units and check arithmetic.

sections.heading: Placement, timing and ISFM
sections.text: Place fertiliser in a band (a line beside the seed), not touching it, and side-dress (apply beside growing plants) later. Split application divides the total rate into doses timed to crop demand, reducing leaching (washing down), volatilisation (gas loss) and lodging (stems falling over). Leaf (foliar) feeding sprays a dilute solution onto leaves for quick correction, mainly micronutrients; it supplements soil application. Integrated soil fertility management (ISFM) combines organic and mineral inputs with improved seed, good agronomy and soil and water conservation, adapted locally. Over-application wastes money and can cause lodging, nutrient imbalance, salinity and acidification. Excess nitrogen may leach as nitrate, volatilise as ammonia or emit nitrous oxide; runoff can cause algal blooms. Match inputs to soil tests or realistic yield targets. The 4R rule is right source, rate, time and place.

keyPoints: Organic manures are bulky or concentrated, variable in composition, slow-release and improve soil organic matter.
Inorganic fertilisers are straight, compound or blended; a grade N-P2O5-K2O gives nutrient percentages by mass.
Product rate = nutrient recommendation ÷ fraction of that nutrient in the product.
Example: 60 kg N/ha from 20-10-10 needs 60 ÷ 0.20 = 300 kg product/ha, which also supplies 30 kg P2O5/ha and 30 kg K2O/ha.
Place fertiliser near roots, split doses to match demand, and use foliar sprays only as a supplement.
ISFM combines organic and mineral inputs with good agronomy; over-application wastes money and risks lodging, salinity, acidification and nutrient pollution.

en.title: Weeds and Weed Management
en.short: Weed classification, competition, control methods, herbicide selectivity and integrated weed management.

sections.heading: Weeds and life cycles
sections.text: Weeds are plants growing where they are not wanted. They are classified by life cycle as annuals (one season), biennials (two seasons) and perennials (more than two years, often with underground stems or tubers). They are also grouped as broadleaf or grass-like. Annuals spread mainly by seed; perennials regrow from vegetative parts. Weeds compete for light, water, nutrients and space, and early competition is often most damaging. They also host pests and diseases, such as aphids, nematodes and rusts, and some release allelopathic chemicals (natural plant toxins) that suppress crops.

sections.heading: Control and herbicides
sections.text: Prevention stops weeds entering the field: clean seed, clean machinery and border hygiene. Cultural control uses crop competition and planning: competitive varieties, narrow rows, timely sowing, fertiliser placement, rotation and cover crops. Mechanical control includes tillage, hand weeding, mowing and cultivation before weeds set seed. Biological control uses living agents such as insects or fungi against specific invasive weeds; it is slow and needs safety testing. Chemical control uses herbicides. Selectivity is the ability to kill weeds without harming the crop. It comes from crop tolerance, placement, timing and formulation. Modes of action include inhibition of photosynthesis, amino acid synthesis, cell division, lipid synthesis and growth regulation. Repeated use of one mode of action selects resistant weeds, so rotate modes of action.

sections.heading: Integrated programme
sections.text: An integrated weed management (IWM) programme combines prevention, cultural, mechanical, biological and chemical methods. Identify the weeds and their life cycles, then set a goal: prevent seed set, reduce the seedbank (stored weed seeds) and protect yield. Use rotation, competitive crops, clean seed and machinery, early seedbed preparation, timely cultivation, and herbicides only when needed. Monitor and keep records. For example, a maize grower who hand-weeds early, rotates with a legume and rotates herbicide modes of action reduces the seedbank and slows resistance.

keyPoints: Weeds are classified by life cycle as annual, biennial or perennial, and as broadleaf or grass-like.
Weeds compete for light, water, nutrients and space and can host pests and diseases.
Prevention and cultural control reduce weed pressure before herbicides are needed.
Herbicide selectivity depends on crop tolerance, placement, timing and formulation.
Rotating herbicide modes of action slows the selection of resistant weeds.
Integrated weed management combines prevention, cultural, mechanical, biological and chemical methods.

en.title: Crop Pests and Integrated Pest Management
en.short: Pest groups, damage signs, economic thresholds, IPM components and pesticide safety.

sections.heading: Pest groups and damage
sections.text: Chewing insects bite leaves, stems or fruit, leaving holes, notches or cut seedlings. Sucking insects and mites pierce tissue and remove sap, causing yellowing, curling, stunting, honeydew and sooty mould; many spread viruses. Boring insects tunnel into stems, cobs, tubers or fruit, leaving entry holes, frass (insect droppings) and dead hearts (dead central shoots). Nematodes are microscopic roundworms; root-knot nematodes cause root galls, while cyst nematodes form small cysts on roots; both cause stunting and yellowing. Rodents gnaw stems, roots, stored grain and seedlings. Birds peck seeds, seedlings and fruit. Inspect roots and stores, not only leaves.

sections.heading: Economic injury level and threshold
sections.text:
The economic injury level (EIL) is the pest density where control cost equals the value of yield loss prevented. Below it, control costs more than it saves. EIL = C ÷ (V × I): C is control cost per unit area, V is crop value per kg, I is yield loss per pest per unit area. Use one area unit. The economic threshold (ET) is the lower density at which control starts, so pests do not reach the EIL; it is a management choice.

Example: C = $25/ha = $0.0025/m²; V = $0.50/kg; I = 0.004 kg/m² per pest. EIL = 0.0025 ÷ (0.50 × 0.004) = 1.25 pests/m². Check: 1.25 × 0.004 = 0.005 kg/m² lost, worth $0.0025/m², or $25/ha. ET = 1 pest/m².

sections.heading: IPM components
sections.text: Integrated pest management (IPM) combines tactics after monitoring and identification. Cultural control uses rotation, sanitation, destruction of crop residues, planting dates, trap crops and balanced water and fertiliser. Biological control uses predators, parasitoids (insects that live in or on other insects and kill them) and pathogens; conserve them by reducing broad-spectrum sprays and keeping habitat. Host resistance uses varieties that resist or tolerate pests. Chemical control uses registered, selective pesticides at the label dose, rotating modes of action and spot spraying only when thresholds justify it.

sections.heading: Pesticide safety
sections.text: Pesticide safety: read the label, wear personal protective equipment, avoid drift, protect pollinators, observe re-entry and pre-harvest intervals, store locked away from food, dispose of containers safely and report poisoning. Use only registered products.

keyPoints: Chewing pests remove tissue, sucking pests remove sap, and boring pests tunnel into stems, cobs or fruit.
Nematodes, rodents and birds often need root, store and seedling checks.
EIL is the density where control cost equals the value of yield loss prevented: EIL = C ÷ (V × I).
ET is the lower action density, usually set by management below the EIL.
IPM combines monitoring, cultural control, biological control, host resistance and selective chemicals.
Pesticide safety requires the label, PPE, re-entry and pre-harvest intervals, safe storage and disposal.

en.title: Crop Diseases and Integrated Disease Management
en.short: Fungal, bacterial, viral, phytoplasma and nematode causes, disease triangle, cycles and integrated management.

sections.heading: Causes and the disease triangle
sections.text: Plant disease is abnormal, harmful change in a crop. Biotic causes are pathogens, meaning disease-causing agents: fungi, bacteria, viruses, phytoplasmas and nematodes. Fungi often grow as threads and spread by spores. Bacteria are single cells and enter through wounds or natural openings. Viruses are tiny agents inside cells, often carried by insects or sap. Phytoplasmas are wall-less bacteria spread mainly by leafhoppers. Nematodes are tiny roundworms; some feed on roots and some transmit viruses. Abiotic disorders, such as nutrient deficiency, are not infectious. The disease triangle says disease develops only when a susceptible host, a virulent pathogen and a favourable environment meet. Virulent means highly able to cause disease. Time is sometimes added as a fourth factor.

sections.heading: Disease cycles and spread
sections.text: A disease cycle is the pathogen’s repeated stages: survival, dispersal, infection, colonisation, symptom expression and reproduction. Infection means the pathogen establishes in the host. Spread may be by wind, water, soil, seed, insects, tools or people. Monocyclic diseases have one cycle per season; polycyclic diseases have many. Epidemics need susceptible tissue, abundant inoculum and suitable weather. Inoculum is the pathogen material that starts infection.

sections.heading: Integrated management
sections.text: Integrated disease management combines methods, with resistant varieties as the base. Cultural control includes clean seed, crop rotation, sanitation, spacing and water management. Biological control uses antagonists, beneficial organisms that suppress pathogens, such as Trichoderma fungi or Bacillus bacteria. Seed treatment protects seed or seedlings, using hot water, biological agents or fungicides. Fungicides are chemicals that kill or suppress fungi; use them when risk justifies it, with correct dose, timing and alternation to limit resistance. For example, a maize farmer in Kaduna notices leaf lesions. Extension advice confirms a fungal leaf blight. She plants a resistant hybrid next season, rotates with cowpea, removes crop debris and applies a recommended fungicide only if weather favours disease. This is integrated management.

keyPoints: The main biotic causes of crop disease are fungi, bacteria, viruses, phytoplasmas and nematodes.
The disease triangle requires a susceptible host, a virulent pathogen and a favourable environment.
A disease cycle describes survival, dispersal, infection, colonisation, symptom expression and reproduction.
Integrated disease management combines resistant varieties, cultural methods, biological control, seed treatment and careful fungicide use.
Fungicides should be used only when risk justifies them, with correct dose, timing and alternation to limit resistance.
Accurate diagnosis matters because fungi, bacteria, viruses, phytoplasmas and nematodes need different controls.

en.title: Crop Responses to Environmental Stress
en.short: How drought, heat, cold, salinity, waterlogging, flooding and wind harm crops, and how farmers reduce stress.

sections.heading: Stress and injury
sections.text: Environmental stress is any abiotic condition that reduces growth below the crop’s potential. Plants often first lose cell turgor, then close stomata, which lowers photosynthesis and growth. Severe or long stress causes injury, reduced yield and sometimes death. The same stress can produce different symptoms at different stages.

sections.heading: Symptoms by stress
sections.text: Drought gives wilting, rolled leaves and grey-green colour; stomata close, photosynthesis falls and leaves senesce. Heat causes leaf scorch and poor pollen viability; membranes and proteins are damaged. Cold causes pale or purplish leaves, stunting and poor germination; membranes leak ions and photosynthesis is inhibited. Salinity causes leaf-tip burn, stunting and patchy stands; osmotic stress reduces water uptake, while sodium or chloride toxicity damages leaves. Waterlogging causes yellowing, epinasty (downward leaf bending) and root decay; roots lack oxygen and anaerobic respiration produces ethanol. Flooding submerges tissue, causing oxygen and light loss, chlorosis and rotting. Wind causes lodging, leaf tearing and sandblasting; it also increases transpiration and can desiccate leaves.

sections.heading: Escape, avoidance, tolerance
sections.text: Plants adapt in three ways. Escape means finishing the life cycle before the stress arrives, as with early-maturing millet. Avoidance means keeping tissue water or temperature safe, through deep roots, stomatal closure, leaf rolling or reduced leaf area. Tolerance means surviving injury with cell adjustments, such as osmotic adjustment (solute accumulation that holds water), heat-shock proteins or antioxidant systems. These strategies overlap and vary by species and stage.

sections.heading: Agronomic responses
sections.text: Agronomic responses include drought-tolerant varieties, adjusted sowing dates, mulching and stress-relief irrigation. Sowing dates are moved so sensitive stages miss peak heat or drought. Mulch reduces evaporation and soil temperature; irrigation relieves drought at flowering or grain filling. In a small case, Amina grows early millet on a sandy field in northern Nigeria. She sows after the first reliable rain, keeps crop residue as mulch and gives one supplementary irrigation at flowering. The early variety escapes late drought, while mulch and irrigation reduce stress at flowering.

keyPoints: Environmental stress reduces growth through water loss, membrane damage, oxygen shortage or physical injury.
Drought causes wilting and leaf rolling, while heat damages membranes and pollen and cold causes ion leakage and stunting.
Salinity combines osmotic stress with ion toxicity, and waterlogging or flooding causes oxygen shortage and root or leaf damage.
Wind causes lodging, abrasion and increased transpiration.
Escape, avoidance and tolerance are overlapping adaptation strategies.
Drought-tolerant varieties, adjusted sowing dates, mulching and stress-relief irrigation reduce risk when matched to local conditions.

en.title: Cropping Systems: Rotation, Intercropping and Relay Cropping
en.short: Sole, mixed, row, relay and sequential cropping, land equivalent ratio, and rotation benefits and costs.

sections.heading: Patterns of cropping
sections.text: Sole cropping means one crop occupies a field for a season. Sequential cropping grows two or more crops one after another on the same land in one year. Intercropping grows two or more crops together. In mixed intercropping crops are sown without distinct rows; in row intercropping they are sown in separate rows, which eases weeding. Relay cropping is intercropping in which a later crop is sown into a standing earlier crop before harvest, using residual moisture and labour.

sections.heading: Land equivalent ratio
sections.text:
The land equivalent ratio (LER) compares intercrop with sole crops. For two crops, LER = (intercrop yield A ÷ sole yield A) + (intercrop yield B ÷ sole yield B). Partial ratios are added. LER above 1 means intercropping uses land more efficiently; below 1 sole cropping is better.

Example: sole maize yields 6 t/ha and sole bean 2 t/ha. Intercropped, they yield 4.2 t/ha maize and 1.1 t/ha bean. Partial LERs are 4.2 ÷ 6 = 0.70 and 1.1 ÷ 2 = 0.55. LER = 1.25, so sole cropping would need 25% more land for the same output.

sections.heading: Rotation: benefits and costs
sections.text: Rotation is a planned sequence of different crops on the same land. It can break weed, pest and disease cycles when the crops are not hosts of the same organisms. It spreads labour and can improve soil structure. Legumes in rotation may add nitrogen through rhizobia, but the amount varies with species, nodulation, residues and management; it is not automatic. Costs include fewer choices of profitable crops, careful planning, and possible yield loss if the sequence is poorly matched. Related crops in sequence may share pests and diseases.

sections.heading: Choosing a system
sections.text: Choice depends on soil, climate, water, labour, machinery, market, food needs and risk. Intercropping suits small farms and risk spreading but complicates spraying and harvesting. Relay cropping suits seasons too short for sequential cropping, or where residual moisture is available. Rotation needs markets and planning. Check local extension advice and current costs.

keyPoints: LER = (intercrop yield of crop A ÷ sole yield of A) + (intercrop yield of crop B ÷ sole yield of B); LER above 1 favours intercropping.
Mixed intercropping has no distinct rows; row intercropping uses separate rows.
Relay cropping sows a second crop into a standing first crop before harvest.
Rotation breaks weed, pest and disease cycles when crops are not hosts of the same organisms.
Legume nitrogen contribution varies and must be managed, not assumed.
Choose a system by soil, climate, labour, market, risk and food needs, and check local advice.

en.title: Agroforestry, Cover Crops and Conservation Agriculture
en.short: This summary covers agroforestry systems, cover crops, mulching and conservation agriculture principles.

sections.heading: Agroforestry systems
sections.text: Agroforestry is the deliberate growing of trees or shrubs with crops or livestock on the same land. In alley cropping, hedgerows of trees or shrubs are planted in rows, often along the contour, and crops grow in the alleys between them. Prunings can be used as mulch. Boundary planting puts trees on field edges, where they mark boundaries and reduce wind. Parkland systems keep scattered mature trees in cropland, as with Faidherbia albida in semi-arid West Africa. Home gardens are small, mixed plots near the house with trees, vegetables and other annuals.

sections.heading: Roles of trees
sections.text: Trees and shrubs modify the crop microclimate. Shade lowers leaf temperature and reduces evaporation, but too much shade reduces light for crops. Windbreaks reduce wind speed, so there is less lodging, sandblast damage and soil erosion. Trees also cycle nutrients: deep roots take up nutrients and litter returns them to the surface. Legumes such as Gliricidia can fix nitrogen, though the amount varies with soil and management.

sections.heading: Cover crops and mulch
sections.text: Cover crops are grown mainly to protect and improve soil, not for harvest. They reduce erosion, suppress weeds and add organic matter. A green manure is a cover crop incorporated while still green so its nutrients become available. Mulching means spreading organic material such as crop residues on the soil surface. Mulch conserves water, moderates soil temperature and reduces splash erosion. Cover crops and mulch must be managed to avoid competition for water and nutrients.

sections.heading: Conservation agriculture
sections.text: Conservation agriculture rests on three principles: minimum soil disturbance, permanent soil cover and crop diversification. Minimum disturbance means no or reduced tillage, with planting through residues. Permanent cover means keeping the soil covered with residues or living plants. Diversification means rotating or intercropping different crops. A small case: Amina grows maize, keeps crop residues as mulch, and rotates with cowpea. This can protect soil, but results depend on rainfall, residue availability and weeds. Check local extension advice.

keyPoints: Agroforestry deliberately combines trees or shrubs with crops or livestock.
Alley cropping, boundary planting, parkland systems and home gardens are common arrangements.
Trees give shade, wind protection and nutrient cycling, but heavy shade can cut crop light.
Cover crops protect soil; green manure is incorporated while green; mulch is spread on the surface.
Conservation agriculture has three principles: minimum soil disturbance, permanent soil cover and crop diversification.
Results depend on local rainfall, soil, weeds and residue supply, so check local advice.

en.title: Pasture and Forage Agronomy
en.short: Forage species, rangeland and improved pasture, grazing management, conserved feed and crop-livestock integration.

sections.heading: Forage species and value
sections.text: Forages are plants grown or managed for grazing, cutting or conservation. Grasses provide bulk and fibre; legumes provide protein and can fix nitrogen with rhizobia. Examples include elephant, guinea and Rhodes grasses, and stylo, centro and lucerne legumes. Growth habit matters: tufted grasses suit cutting, stoloniferous or rhizomatous types spread and cover soil, and twining legumes mix with grasses. Nutritive value means protein, energy, digestibility and intake; it falls as plants mature and fibre rises. Legumes raise protein but may cause bloat (gas build-up), so introduce them carefully.

sections.heading: Rangeland and improved pasture
sections.text: Natural rangeland is grazed land dominated by native or self-regenerating vegetation, usually with low inputs and variable feed supply. Improved pasture is sown, fertilised and managed for higher, more reliable output. Rangeland suits extensive communal or ranching systems; improved pasture costs more and needs good establishment. Establishment requires a suitable species, good seed, a firm weed-free seedbed, correct sowing depth and legume inoculation where needed. Control grazing until plants are well rooted.

sections.heading: Stocking and grazing
sections.text: Stocking rate is the number of animals on an area for a period; carrying capacity is the sustainable stocking rate the pasture can support without decline. Rotational grazing moves animals between paddocks, giving grazed plants rest to regrow. Example: a pasture yields 8,000 kg dry matter per hectare per year. Assume animals can use 60% of it, so usable forage is 4,800 kg per hectare. One 450 kg animal unit eats about 2.5% of its body weight as dry matter daily: 450 × 0.025 = 11.25 kg/day, or 11.25 × 365 = 4,106 kg/year. Carrying capacity ≈ 4,800 ÷ 4,106 = 1.17 animal units per hectare. Definitions vary, so use local figures.

sections.heading: Conserved feed and integration
sections.text: Hay is cut forage dried to a safe moisture level for storage; silage is cut forage preserved by anaerobic fermentation, usually at higher moisture. Both bridge dry-season feed gaps. Crop-livestock integration uses crop residues for feed and manure for soil fertility, and can include fodder banks or ley rotations. It raises whole-farm efficiency but needs careful timing, storage and animal health management.

keyPoints: Forages are grasses or legumes grown for grazing, cutting or conservation; legumes usually have more protein and grasses more fibre.
Natural rangeland is low-input grazed native vegetation; improved pasture is sown and managed for higher output.
Stocking rate = animals per unit area per period; carrying capacity = sustainable stocking rate.
Carrying capacity ≈ usable dry matter per hectare ÷ dry matter intake per animal per year.
Rotational grazing rests paddocks so grazed plants can regrow.
Hay is dried forage; silage is anaerobically fermented forage; crop-livestock integration uses residues and manure.

en.title: Soil Conservation and Erosion Control
en.short: Water and wind erosion, risk factors, control practices and field soil-loss assessment.

sections.heading: Erosion processes
sections.text: Erosion is the detachment and transport of soil by water or wind. Water erosion begins with raindrop splash, then sheet flow, rills and gullies. Wind erosion moves particles by saltation (bouncing), suspension (fine dust) and surface creep (rolling). Both remove the topsoil first. Topsoil holds most organic matter, nutrients and roots, so its loss lowers fertility, water storage and yield. Deposition elsewhere can also bury crops and silt channels.

sections.heading: Risk factors
sections.text: Risk rises with intense rain, strong wind, bare ground, long or steep slopes, weak soil structure, low organic matter, compaction and fine sandy or silty surfaces. Tillage that leaves no cover, overgrazing and removing residues also raise risk. Soil loss is worst when erosive events coincide with bare, freshly cultivated soil.

sections.heading: Control practices
sections.text: Contour farming runs tillage and crop rows across the slope, shortening flow paths. Strip cropping alternates row crops with close-growing strips that trap soil. Terracing uses embankments or channels to hold runoff and soil on long slopes. Grass waterways carry concentrated runoff safely. Mulches protect the surface from raindrops and wind. Cover crops cover bare soil between main crops. Shelterbelts, rows of trees or shrubs, slow wind and trap blown soil. These practices work best together.

sections.heading: Assessing soil loss
sections.text: Field assessment uses signs such as rills, exposed roots, pedestals (soil columns left standing under stones or plants) and sediment fans, plus runoff plots or erosion pins. Models estimate average annual loss from water erosion. The Universal Soil Loss Equation is A = R × K × LS × C × P, where A is soil loss, R rainfall erosivity, K soil erodibility, LS slope length and steepness, C cover management and P support practice. Example: R = 300, K = 0.03, LS = 2, C = 0.2, P = 0.5. Then A = 300 × 0.03 × 2 × 0.2 × 0.5 = 1.8 tonnes per hectare per year. Without the support practice (P = 1), loss is 3.6. Models need local calibration; check local soil-loss tolerance.

keyPoints: Erosion detaches and transports soil, removing nutrient-rich topsoil first.
Water erosion moves through splash, sheet, rill and gully stages; wind erosion by saltation, suspension and creep.
Bare soil, steep or long slopes, intense rain or wind and low organic matter raise risk.
Contour farming, strip cropping, terracing, grass waterways, mulches, cover crops and shelterbelts reduce erosion.
USLE: A = R × K × LS × C × P estimates average annual soil loss from water erosion.
Check local calibration and soil-loss tolerance before interpreting model results.

en.title: Crop Harvesting, Threshing and Postharvest Handling
en.short: Maturity indices, harvest methods, threshing, drying, storage pests and postharvest loss reduction.

sections.heading: Maturity and harvest
sections.text: Harvest maturity indices are observable signs that a crop has reached the stage for its intended use. For cereals, check grain hardness, husk or cob colour, and dry matter; in maize, the black layer at the kernel base marks physiological maturity. For grain legumes, pods turn yellow or brown, seeds become hard, and a few rattle. For roots and tubers, wait for leaf senescence and skin set, when the skin does not rub off easily, and for adequate dry matter. Perennial crops such as coffee, cocoa, oil palm and banana are picked selectively by colour, size, firmness or oil or sugar content. Harvest method depends on scale, terrain, labour and loss risk. Cereals use sickles, reapers or combines; legumes are pulled or cut and threshed gently to avoid shattering; roots are lifted with forks or diggers; perennials need repeated selective picking.

sections.heading: Threshing and drying
sections.text: Threshing separates grain from cobs, pods or panicles. Winnowing removes chaff and dust by wind or fan. Dry promptly and evenly, on tarpaulins or in dryers, to avoid mould and cracking. Moisture content wet basis is (wet weight − dry weight) ÷ wet weight × 100. Example: a 100 g sample dries to 86 g, so moisture = (100 − 86) ÷ 100 × 100 = 14 per cent. Safe storage moisture is crop-specific and climate-specific; for many cereals it is near 12 to 14 per cent wet basis, but check local extension advice.

sections.heading: Storage and losses
sections.text: Store in clean, dry, pest-proof structures: sacks on pallets, cribs, airtight hermetic bags or silos. Pests include weevils, bruchids (legume weevils), rodents and birds; moulds also grow on damp grain and some produce aflatoxins. Control by hygiene, drying, hermetic storage, approved insecticides and monitoring. Losses occur at harvest, threshing, drying, storage and transport as spillage, breakage, insect damage and mould. Agronomic practice reduces them: sow adapted varieties, harvest on time, thresh gently, dry promptly, store properly and inspect regularly.

keyPoints: Harvest maturity indices differ by crop; use several signs and the intended use.
Timely harvest and gentle handling reduce shattering, cracking and mould.
Threshing separates grain from cobs or pods; winnowing removes chaff.
Moisture content wet basis = (wet weight − dry weight) ÷ wet weight × 100.
Dry to a crop-specific safe moisture before storage; check local advice.
Clean, dry, pest-proof storage and regular inspection cut postharvest losses.

en.title: Crop Quality, Grading and Product Standards
en.short: Quality attributes, sampling and grading, standards bodies, export rules and how management shapes quality.

sections.heading: What buyers measure
sections.text:
Buyers judge a lot by measurable attributes. Grain size and colour indicate variety, maturity and cleanliness. Moisture content is the mass of water as a share of total mass, on a wet basis. Foreign matter is anything that is not the crop, such as stones, chaff or other seeds. Damage includes broken, insect-damaged, diseased or discoloured grains. Protein and oil content matter for food, feed and processing.

Moisture example: 1,000 g of grain at 20% moisture contains 200 g water and 800 g dry matter. Dry to 14% wet basis: water = (0.14 ÷ 0.86) × 800 = 130.2 g. Total mass = 930.2 g. Water removed = 69.8 g. Check: 130.2 ÷ 930.2 = 14.0%.

sections.heading: Grading and sampling
sections.text:
A grade is a class, such as Grade 1 or Grade 2, defined by limits for moisture, foreign matter, damage and other attributes. Grading is only as good as the sample. A representative sample is taken from several places in the lot, mixed, and reduced by a sample divider or by quartering (dividing into quarters and keeping opposite quarters). Standards state sample size, test methods and allowed limits (tolerances).

National standards bodies set grades and test methods. Examples include the Standards Organisation of Nigeria (SON) and the Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS). Export quality is also governed by the contract and the importing country’s rules. These may require phytosanitary (plant health) certificates and set limits for aflatoxin (a mould toxin) or pesticide residues. Limits differ by country and crop, so check the current official standard.

sections.heading: How management shapes quality
sections.text:
Variety sets the potential for size, colour, protein and oil. Fertiliser changes it: nitrogen usually raises cereal protein, while in oilseeds extra nitrogen often raises protein and can lower oil. Harvest timing matters. Early harvest gives immature, high-moisture grain. Late harvest risks shattering, weathering, sprouting and discolouration. Pests and diseases cause damage and toxins.

So quality is made in the field and protected after harvest. Match variety and inputs to the market, sample honestly, and grade against the current standard.

keyPoints: Moisture content (wet basis) = water mass ÷ total mass × 100.
When drying, water after = (target moisture ÷ (1 − target moisture)) × dry matter, with moisture as a decimal.
A representative sample is the basis of any grade.
National standards bodies set grades; export contracts and importing-country rules also apply.
Variety, nitrogen and harvest timing all shift quality.
High moisture and damage raise storage and toxin risk.

en.title: Crop Improvement, Variety Release and Seed Systems
en.short: Breeding methods, variety testing and release, seed classes, certification and farmer seed systems.

sections.heading: Breeding methods
sections.text:
Plant breeding changes crops to suit farmers and markets. In self-pollinated crops, pure-line selection chooses single plants and keeps stable offspring. Cross-pollinated crops use mass or recurrent selection. Hybridisation crosses two parents to combine traits. A hybrid variety is the first-generation (F1) offspring of two inbred parents; it is uniform and often high-yielding, but saved seed loses performance.

Mutation breeding exposes seed or tissue to a mutagen, often radiation, and selects useful variants. Polyploidy means more than two chromosome sets; breeders induce it, often with colchicine, to create extra sets, sometimes giving larger fruits or sterility.

sections.heading: Selection criteria
sections.text:
Selection criteria are yield, quality, maturity and resistance. Yield is measured in replicated trials, with each line in several plots. Quality covers grain size, taste, oil content or fibre strength. Maturity must fit the rainfall season and labour calendar. Resistance to pests and diseases reduces losses.

Example: 40 maize lines are tested at two sites for two seasons. Line A yields 5.2 t/ha against the check (a standard variety grown for comparison) at 4.5 t/ha but matures one week later. In a short-rainfall area the check may still be safer.

sections.heading: Testing and release
sections.text:
Before release, a candidate variety goes through variety testing. Distinctness, uniformity and stability (DUS) checks show it is different from existing varieties, uniform and stable. Value for cultivation and use (VCU) trials compare yield and quality with local checks across locations and years.

A national release body then decides. Rules differ by country, so check the national seed authority.

sections.heading: Seed systems
sections.text:
Released seed is multiplied in common classes: breeder, foundation, registered and certified seed. Each class comes from the one before. Certification is official inspection and testing of seed fields and lots for purity, germination and health.

The formal seed system links breeders, seed companies, certifiers and agrodealers. The farmer seed system is seed saved, exchanged or bought locally. It supplies most seed in many African countries. Formal seed gives guaranteed quality; farmer seed gives access, low cost and local adaptation.

keyPoints: Plant breeding changes crop populations; selection, hybridisation, mutation and polyploidy are its main tools.
A hybrid variety is F1 seed from two inbred parents, and saved seed usually loses yield and uniformity.
Breeders judge lines on yield, quality, maturity and resistance, using replicated trials and local checks.
DUS and VCU trials support variety release, but release rules are country-specific.
Seed classes commonly run from breeder to foundation, registered and certified seed, each multiplied from the previous class.
Formal seed systems offer certified quality, while farmer seed systems offer access and local adaptation, and both are needed.

en.title: Farm Planning, Field Budgets and Machinery Management
en.short: Enterprise budgets, gross margins, cropping-plan choice, field capacity, machinery costs and labour calendars.

sections.heading: Budgets and gross margins
sections.text: An enterprise budget is a planned statement for one crop. It lists expected output, variable costs and fixed costs. Variable costs change with area: seed, fertiliser, sprays, casual labour, fuel. Fixed costs do not: machinery depreciation, land rent, permanent labour. Gross margin is gross output minus variable costs. It measures return to fixed resources, not profit. Compare gross margins per hectare when land limits, or per unit of labour or capital when those limit. Example: maize output 600, variable costs 400, gross margin 200 per ha. Soybean output 500, variable costs 250, gross margin 250. If land is fixed and both are feasible, soybean is preferred by 50 per ha. Check labour, cash, rotation and risk before deciding.

sections.heading: Field operations and capacity
sections.text:
